    Feeling All the Feels: Crash Course Psychology #25

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • The James-Lange, Cannon-Bard and two-factor models, and what each puts first
    • Why facial expressions are not simple read-outs of inner emotion
    • How context and interpretation change what the same bodily arousal means
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Status, partly holds as a family of models, checked Oct 2026. Classic theories are models, not rival brain boxes. James and Lange put bodily feedback first; Cannon argued that visceral changes are too slow and too undifferentiated, proposing central processing; Schachter and Singer made arousal plus situational interpretation the key. Modern accounts borrow pieces from all three rather than awarding one a total victory.
    • Barrett changes the question. The theory of constructed emotion says the brain regulates the body for allostasis, then uses predictions and learned concepts to categorise sensory changes. The 2016 account is not saying emotion is fake. It says anger, fear and joy are constructed events, not fixed packages waiting in one brain location.
    • The Ekman universality claim has a methods problem. Ekman and colleagues used posed faces, emotion words and forced-choice tasks that can teach participants the categories being tested. Gendron, Roberson, van der Vyver and Barrett (2014) found that Himba participants did not show the predicted universal sorting without emotion-concept cues; with cues, the sorts moved closer, but substantial variation remained. Later review work argues that discovery-based tasks weaken the universality thesis, not that faces carry no useful information.
    • Reading emotions needs a humility rule. Face movements can communicate, regulate an interaction and sometimes correlate with emotion, but they do not identify a person's private state with certainty. This is the bridge to No. 06, Read the room: combine face, voice, words, context and a check-in. For a web pitch, treat a client's expression as a prompt to ask, not permission to mind-read.
    William James1842-1910. His 1884 emotion essay made bodily feedback central to the James-Lange tradition.
    Lisa Feldman BarrettBorn 1963. Developed the theory of constructed emotion and the role of prediction, interoception and concepts.

    "I can read that as a signal, but not as a diagnosis. What else in the situation would confirm it?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: why is a face not a reliable emotion meter?

    Compare with a model answer
    A facial movement is an observable action, not a private emotion label. The same smile or tense brow can fit several situations, and people learn emotion concepts through language and culture. Body state, context, voice, history and the person's own report improve the inference. Ask before you conclude.

    What does James-Lange put first?

    Show answer
    A stimulus produces bodily changes, and the felt perception of those changes is the emotion.

    What are Schachter and Singer's two factors?

    Show answer
    Physiological arousal and a cognitive interpretation of what that arousal means in context.

    What did the Himba study challenge?

    Show answer
    It challenged the idea that posed facial expressions have universally recognised emotion meanings independent of concepts and context.

    A safari lodge client says your new price page feels aggressive because one team member looks tense in a review call. How do you respond?

    Show a model answer
    Do not accept either reading as a fact. Ask what in the page or call produced that impression, check the words and the context, and invite the teammate to say what they meant. Emotion science supports a testable conversation, not a facial lie detector.

    Metaethics: Crash Course Philosophy #32

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • The difference between normative ethics and metaethics
    • Realism, relativism, error theory and expressivism as answers to the same moral sentence
    • Why facts about human wellbeing do not by themselves settle the metaethical question
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Status, survey evidence only, checked Oct 2026. The 2020 PhilPapers survey is a snapshot, not a census of humanity. Among 1,719 respondents who answered the realism question, 62.07 percent accepted or leaned toward moral realism and 26.12 percent toward anti-realism. On a more fine-grained question with 1,024 respondents, naturalist realism was 31.64 percent, non-naturalism 26.56 percent, constructivism 20.80 percent, expressivism 10.64 percent and error theory 5.27 percent. The survey itself warns against treating these numbers as a simple time trend.
    • Mackie's error theory is stronger than cynicism. It says moral language purports to describe objective, intrinsically motivating facts, but the world contains no such queer facts. The conclusion is error, not that anything goes. A business can still use contracts, policies and justified criticism without pretending that its policy is written into the universe.
    • Haidt's moral foundations theory moved the debate into psychology. The original five were care or harm, fairness or reciprocity, loyalty, authority and purity. Graham, Haidt and Nosek (2009) reported that liberals weighted care and fairness more, while conservatives used all five more evenly. A 2020 meta-analysis found the basic pattern but also moderate heterogeneity, self-selection concerns and cultural variation.
    • The measurement is contested. A 2020 systematic analysis of 539 studies using the Moral Foundations Questionnaire found that 38 percent reported no reliability estimate, and mean reliability for four of five subscales was below .70. Later MFQ-2 work separates equality and proportionality and tests more populations. Moral intuitions are useful data, not a final map of moral reality.
    J. L. Mackie1917-1981. Defended error theory in Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong (1977).
    Jonathan HaidtBorn 1963. Moral psychologist and co-author of the 2009 moral-foundations work.

    "Before we fight about the verdict, let us say what kind of moral claim we think we are making."

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: distinguish realism, error theory and expressivism.

    Compare with a model answer
    Realism says some moral claims are true independently of our attitudes. Error theory agrees that ordinary moral claims aim at objective truth but says they are all false because the required facts do not exist. Expressivism says moral language primarily expresses commitments or attitudes and guides action rather than reporting stance-independent facts.

    What does metaethics ask?

    Show answer
    It asks what moral claims mean, whether moral facts exist, and how moral knowledge or motivation could work.

    What is Mackie's error theory?

    Show answer
    Moral claims purport to report objective facts, but no such facts exist, so ordinary moral claims are systematically in error.

    Name Haidt's original five foundations.

    Show answer
    Care or harm, fairness or reciprocity, loyalty, authority and purity or sanctity.

    A client wants callers paid commission only when a lead closes, even if the caller did honest qualification work. How do you make the disagreement productive?

    Show a model answer
    Separate the levels. At the normative level, compare fairness, incentives and consequences. At the metaethical level, notice whether the team treats fairness as a shared rule, an expression of respect or a fact that should bind everyone. Then write a transparent policy and test its effects rather than hiding a value choice inside a spreadsheet.

    Kant & Categorical Imperatives: Crash Course Philosophy #35

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • The difference between hypothetical and categorical imperatives
    • The universal-law, humanity and kingdom-of-ends formulations

    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Status, the framework holds but the hard case remains contested, checked Oct 2026. Kant tests maxims, not slogans, and his famous case is genuinely hard. The same outward act can have different maxims, so ask what policy the agent is choosing and why. In On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropic Motives, Kant denies a right to lie even to a murderer and worries that the liar may be responsible for unforeseeable consequences. This is a real tension, not a classroom myth. Do not soften it into Kant secretly being a consequentialist.
    • Korsgaard's reply is more careful than a simple rescue. In The Right to Lie (1986), she argues that the universal-law analysis can permit the particular lie when the maxim is properly specified, while the humanity and kingdom-of-ends perspectives explain why Kant treats lying as wrong in the ideal of relations between rational agents. Her larger conclusion is that a moral system may need special principles for dealing with evil. Other Kantians, including Cholbi, also argue that self-defence and the duty to protect rational nature can support deception in this case.
    • Indian duty ethics is a comparison, not a translation. In the Bhagavad Gita 2.47, Krishna tells Arjuna to perform his duty without attachment to its fruits and without retreating into inaction. Nishkama karma resembles Kant in disciplining motive and detaching action from reward, but dharma is role, cosmic and relational, while Kant grounds obligation in autonomous rational law. The Gita does not simply say Kant in Sanskrit.
    • Kant's racism must stay in the picture. His writings and lectures on race include explicit hierarchical claims, from essays beginning in 1775 through the 1798 Anthropology. Scholars disagree about how tightly those claims infect his moral and political philosophy: some distinguish universal moral personhood from racist anthropology, while others argue the hierarchy persists and exposes limits in his universalism. The honest method is neither cancellation nor sanitisation: read the ethical argument, name the contradiction and ask what a genuinely universal principle must reject.
    Immanuel Kant1724-1804. Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785) and the essay on lying (1797).
    Christine KorsgaardBorn 1952. Kant scholar whose 1986 essay The Right to Lie addresses evil, maxims and the murderer case.

    "What is my maxim, and could I defend it if every person used it against me?"

    Compare with a model answer
    State the action as a maxim, including the purpose that makes it intelligible. Ask whether you could conceive and will that maxim as a universal law. Then check whether the action respects every person as an end rather than merely using them. The test targets principles of agency, not a quick count of consequences.

    What is a maxim?

    Show answer
    The practical principle or policy a person acts on, including the purpose that makes the action intelligible.

    Name Kant's three formulations used here.

    Show answer
    Universal law, humanity as an end, and the kingdom of ends.

    What is nishkama karma?

    Show answer
    Action done as duty without attachment to the fruits or results, while avoiding the opposite error of inaction.

    A client asks you to hide a known limitation in a clinic website until after payment. What would Kant ask, and what should you do?

    Show a model answer
    State the maxim: I will conceal material information when disclosure threatens a sale. Universalising it destroys honest consent, and it treats the client and patients as means. Disclose the limitation in plain language, document the decision and offer a remedy. A short-term conversion win is not a licence to use people.

    Utilitarianism: Crash Course Philosophy #36

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • Bentham's greatest-happiness principle and the problem of adding pleasures
    • Mill's higher pleasures and Singer's expanding circle of concern
    • How trolley problems and the FTX collapse expose the gap between a rule and its practice
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Status, useful decision lens but not a complete moral licence, checked Oct 2026. Bentham made utility calculable in principle, while Mill rejects a flat pleasure meter. Bentham proposes dimensions including intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity and purity. Mill argues that competent judges can prefer some pleasures qualitatively, especially intellectual and moral ones. Singer then applies equal consideration to distant suffering: his drowning-child argument says distance and the number of other potential helpers do not by themselves erase an avoidable duty to help.
    • Effective altruism is a practice, not a guarantee of virtue. Its core idea is to use evidence and reasoning to compare opportunities to help. Sam Bankman-Fried made the movement's public image an uncomfortable stress test: the US Department of Justice says he was convicted of fraud-related offences, sentenced to 25 years in 2024 and ordered to forfeit $11 billion after misappropriating billions in FTX customer funds. The lesson is not that calculating impact causes fraud. It is that impressive ends, donations or claimed long-term benefits cannot substitute for honesty, governance and constraints on means.
    • Trolley intuitions are data about judgement, not a moral calculator. Awad et al. (2018) collected 40 million decisions from millions of people in 233 countries and territories through the Moral Machine. Globally, participants tended to spare humans over animals, more lives over fewer and younger people over older people, while preferences varied across countries and demographics. The sample is huge, but an opt-in online dilemma is not a mandate for an autonomous vehicle policy.
    • The business version needs rules as well as totals. A pricing decision can maximise next month's cash by hiding a fee, but destroy trust and harm callers who rely on honest commissions. Use expected impact, include uncertainty and long-run trust, and set side-constraints: no deception, no stealing, no quietly externalising risk. Utilitarian reasoning is strongest when its numbers are inspectable and its blind spots are named.
    Jeremy Bentham1748-1832. Founder of classical utilitarianism and author of the 1789 Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation.
    Peter SingerBorn 1946. Developed influential arguments about distant suffering and effective giving, including Famine, Affluence, and Morality (1972).

    "Whose wellbeing did we count, what did we leave out, and what rule stops the shortcut from becoming abuse?"

The case against simple maximisation is that rights, trust, uncertainty and distribution can disappear inside one total. Use consequence analysis with explicit constraints and transparent assumptions.

    You can raise prices by 8 percent with a hidden renewal clause, or explain the full cost and accept slower growth. What would a serious utilitarian analysis do?

    Show a model answer
    Count immediate revenue, client affordability, support load, caller commissions, churn, referrals and long-run trust. Include the risk that the hidden clause harms people who miss it. If transparent pricing produces less short-term utility but protects many clients and the firm's reliability, it may be the better outcome. In any case, do not hide the assumption or call one metric morality.

    Aristotle & Virtue Theory

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • The function argument and why eudaimonia means activity, not just a pleasant feeling
    • The golden mean as a context-sensitive target, not a bland compromise
    • How habit, role models and phronesis turn a rule into a judgement
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Eudaimonia is activity, not a mood. Aristotle treats flourishing as excellent activity over a complete life, and says ethics is for improving action, not merely collecting theory. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy account stresses that practical wisdom cannot be reduced to memorising rules: it is a trained ability to see what this occasion requires.
    • The mean is not moderation for its own sake. The courageous response can be intense, and the generous response can be large. The target is relative to us and the case, set by the practically wise person. That makes the theory useful for a founder choosing between cowardly avoidance and reckless expansion, but it also leaves hard judgement work unresolved.
    • Confucius gives a real parallel, not a translation. Confucian ren is often rendered humaneness or authoritative conduct, and the junzi is the exemplary person formed through learning, relationships and ritual practice. Aristotle's phronimos and Confucius's junzi can illuminate each other, but scholars warn that li, role and family make the traditions importantly different. See May Sim's comparative study.
    • VIA is a measurement project, not proof that 24 virtues exist. McGrath's 2022 review reports construct-validity evidence across five samples totalling 7,924 adults, with exceptions. That is evidence for particular measures, not a final map of character. Miller's critique notes missing vices, conflicts between strengths, weak links to motivation, no practical-wisdom strength, and factor analyses that do not reliably recover six virtues. See McGrath 2022 and Miller 2018.
    Aristotle384-322 BCE. Nicomachean Ethics makes virtue, practical reasoning, friendship and flourishing a single ethical project.
    Confucius551-479 BCE, traditionally. The Analects presents the junzi as a person formed by learning, ritual, relationships and humane conduct.

    "Which virtue is this decision rehearsing, and what would the practically wise version look like?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: why is Aristotle's golden mean not a call to split the difference?

    Compare with a model answer
    The mean is a fitting response relative to the situation, not a numerical midpoint. Courage can require a dangerous act, while recklessness is excessive and cowardice deficient. Practical wisdom reads the stakes, motives and people involved. Repeatedly choosing that fitting response builds a character disposition, so future choices become easier and more reliable.

    What does eudaimonia mean for Aristotle?

    Show answer
    Flourishing: excellent rational activity across a whole life, not a temporary feeling of pleasure.

    What does phronesis add to a rule?

    Show answer
    Practical wisdom judges what the situation calls for, including when and how a general virtue applies.

    How does VIA differ from Aristotle?

    Show answer
    VIA operationalises proposed character strengths in psychological measures. It can provide data, but its categories and six-virtue structure remain debated and do not replace practical wisdom.

    You are deciding whether to accept a lucrative wildlife client whose campaign would exaggerate conservation results. What would Aristotle and Confucius ask you to practise?

    Show a model answer
    Aristotle would ask which character the deal rehearses, then use phronesis to balance courage, honesty, loyalty and the real consequences. Confucius would add role and relationship: what does a trustworthy junzi owe clients, staff and the public? A good answer may be a candid counter-proposal, not a heroic refusal or a quiet lie.

    Existentialism

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • Why Kierkegaard makes subjective commitment different from merely possessing information
    • Sartre's existence precedes essence and the waiter as an example of bad faith
    • How Beauvoir adds ambiguity and reciprocity, while Camus answers absurdity with revolt
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • There is no single existentialism. The Stanford Encyclopedia overview places Kierkegaard and Nietzsche among the precursors, then distinguishes the religious and secular, freedom-centred and relational strands. Only Sartre and Beauvoir explicitly self-identified as existentialists in the usual French group; Camus rejected the label.
    • Bad faith is not ordinary lying to someone else. Sartre describes a person hiding their freedom by treating a role as a fixed essence, or treating freedom as if it erased every constraint. The concept is ethically useful for a founder who says the market, investors or a client made him betray his stated values, but it can become a blunt accusation unless the real constraints are named.
    • Beauvoir makes freedom relational and ambiguous. A choice is made from a situation, and my freedom is entangled with other people's freedom. This is why her ethics is more than Sartre's lone chooser: a director cannot create freely by treating collaborators as props. The existentialist tradition is heterogeneous, and the Oxford overview of its style and substance warns against reducing it to nihilism.
    • Frankl needs historical honesty. Frankl had developed logotherapy before the war. He and his wife were deported to Theresienstadt in September 1942; research on his life reports imprisonment in four camps, including Auschwitz, Dachau and Türkheim, until liberation in 1945, with the deaths of his wife and parents. A 2021 psychobiographical study is evidence about his documented life and interpretation, not proof that every prisoner could choose meaning or that suffering is secretly beneficial. See Bushkin, van Niekerk and Stroud 2021.
    Soren Kierkegaard1813-1855. Religious precursor who made inward commitment and the existing individual central.
    Simone de Beauvoir1908-1986. Existential philosopher and writer who developed an ethics of ambiguity, reciprocity and situated freedom.

    "Which constraint is real, which excuse is convenient, and what responsibility remains?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: what is Sartre's bad faith?

    Compare with a model answer
    Bad faith is self-deception about freedom. Someone treats a role, job title or social script as a fixed essence, or pretends that freedom means having no constraints. Sartre's point is not that circumstances are unreal. It is that we still interpret and answer them, so saying the role made the choice can hide responsibility.

    How is absurdism different from existentialism?

    Show answer
    Camus's absurdism names the clash between our demand for meaning and an indifferent world, then recommends lucid revolt. Existentialism is a broader, diverse family about existence, freedom, responsibility and meaning.

    What is bad faith?

    Show answer
    A way of hiding one's situated freedom by treating a role, excuse or circumstance as a fixed essence that removes responsibility.

    What is the honest claim about Frankl's camps?

    Show answer
    He was imprisoned in four camps from 1942 to 1945 and later interpreted survival through meaning. His prewar logotherapy predates the camps, and his story cannot be turned into a universal promise that meaning defeats oppression.

    A client asks you to make a wildlife resort look sustainable while hiding its water use. You want the money and the director credit. How would the four thinkers sharpen the decision?

    Show a model answer
    Kierkegaard asks what commitment you can inwardly own, not merely explain. Sartre asks whether you are hiding behind the agency role. Beauvoir asks what your choice enables or denies for workers, visitors and local communities. Camus asks you to face the ugly facts without a comforting story. The honest move is to offer a truthful redesign or decline.

    What Is a Good Life?

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • Nozick's experience machine and the difference between feeling happy and being a certain person doing things
    • The hedonic and eudaimonic traditions, including why relationships and purpose resist a single happiness score
    • How a good life can be tested against your real trade-offs: money, travel, art, health and people
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Nozick's machine is a challenge, not a knockout proof. In the original thought experiment, all experiences are pleasurable but disconnected from actually doing things, being a certain person and contacting reality. An empirical study found about 30 percent chose the machine in a bare scenario, so the intuition is not universal; other versions are affected by status quo and framing. See Hindriks and Douven 2017.
    • Ryff made eudaimonic well-being measurable. Her 1989 framework identifies self-acceptance, positive relations, autonomy, environmental mastery, purpose in life and personal growth. These dimensions are not a claim that one questionnaire settles the good life, but they stop a founder from equating a good month of mood with a whole life.
    • The income story is now a measurement lesson. Kahneman and Deaton analysed more than 450,000 US responses in 2010 and reported life evaluation rising with log income while emotional well-being flattened around 75,000 dollars. Killingsworth's 2021 study used 1,725,994 real-time reports from 33,391 employed US adults and found experienced well-being kept rising with log income. The 2023 adversarial collaboration found both patterns: flattening for roughly the least happy 15 to 20 percent, continued increases for happier groups, and a weak overall association. These are US observational results, not a personal salary target. See Kahneman and Deaton 2010, Killingsworth 2021 and Killingsworth, Kahneman and Mellers 2023.
    • Relationships and plural ends beat a single maximand. The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed people across decades; its public-facing synthesis argues that good relationships are strongly tied to health and happiness, while its original cohorts were not fully representative. An Indian parallel is the four purusarthas: dharma (right conduct), artha (material prosperity), kama (desire and pleasure) and moksha (liberation). Scholars debate whether the category originally names goals or domains of beneficial activity, so use it as a plural map, not a timeless checklist. See Harvard Study of Adult Development and Sharma on purusharthas, with the historical caution in Olivelle 2019.
    Robert Nozick1938-2002. Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) introduced the experience machine thought experiment.
    Carol RyffPsychologist whose 1989 model operationalised six dimensions of psychological well-being beyond pleasure and life satisfaction.

    "Which metric are we optimising: a feeling, a life, a relationship, or a value?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: why is a good life not reducible to happiness in the moment?

    Compare with a model answer
    Momentary happiness matters, but a life can also be judged by what its person does, becomes and sustains. Nozick's machine tests whether pleasure alone is enough. Ryff adds purpose, growth, autonomy, mastery, self-acceptance and relationships. A credible good-life plan therefore tracks feelings alongside agency, meaning, health, relationships and ethical responsibility.

    What is the hedonic versus eudaimonic distinction?

    Show answer
    Hedonic well-being concerns pleasure and feeling good. Eudaimonic well-being concerns functioning and flourishing through purpose, growth, relationships, agency and virtue.

    What did the 2023 income collaboration find?

    Show answer
    The average linear rise and the flattening result can both appear: flattening is concentrated among the least happy roughly 15 to 20 percent, while happier groups keep rising or accelerate. The overall income association is real but weak.

    Name two of Ryff's six dimensions.

    Show answer
    Any two of self-acceptance, positive relations, autonomy, environmental mastery, purpose in life and personal growth.

    You want enough MTRX income to travel as a nomad, enough time to write, and eventually the stamina to direct a film. How do you stop a bigger revenue number from silently becoming your definition of success?

    Show a model answer
    Write a dashboard with four columns: experienced well-being, eudaimonic work, relationships and ethics. Track sleep and delight, hours writing or directing, time with people who matter, and whether client work is truthful and useful. Money remains a means for autonomy and travel, not the sole score. Revisit the dashboard quarterly, because a life is a trajectory, not a launch metric.

    Kanttreat people as ends, never only as tools"Would this still be right if everyone did it?"
    Utilitarianismcount consequences, including the people hidden by the average"Who gains, who pays, and what are we missing?"
    Aristotlerepeated choices train a character"What virtue is this decision rehearsing?"
    Existentialismown your situated freedom instead of hiding behind the script"What responsibility remains?"
    The good lifea good life tracks feeling, flourishing, relationships and values"Which metric are we optimising, and why?"

    Boss fight, optional 15 min: write your operating philosophy for running MTRX for the next three years. Use at least one idea from each week of this guide. Make it operational: name two decisions it would change, one metric it would refuse to optimise, and one rule for what you do when money, growth and integrity conflict.

    Show a model answer
    Model answer: I will run MTRX as a truth-seeking studio that makes useful work without pretending certainty. From Week 1, I will separate evidence from confidence and test claims with small pilots. From Week 2, I will remember that perception, memory and AI outputs are fallible, so I will show limits and keep call records. From Week 3, I will treat identity and social influence as pressures, not destiny, and build a team where dissent is safe. From Week 4, I will use Kant to refuse deceptive sustainability claims, Aristotle to practise honesty and courage until they are habits, existentialism to own choices made under constraint, and the good-life lens to protect writing, health, friendship and travel alongside revenue. I will change a decision when the evidence changes, but I will not optimise growth by making clients or staff less free. My dashboard will include profit, truthful client outcomes, creative hours, health and relationship time. A business that grows while training me to lie is a failed business, even if the monthly number rises.

    CalibrationCalibration: re-rate the Day 1 baseline from 1 to 5. Could you now explain psychology and philosophy to a CEO in a way that is accurate, useful and honest about uncertainty, then use one idea from each week to improve a real decision? Write one sentence about what changed since your original rating.

    Glossary · Weeks 1-2 + map

    Field glossary

    AbductionPhilosophy

    Inference to the best explanation.

    AbsurdPhilosophy

    the clash between a demand for meaning and an indifferent world

    Ad hoc rescuePhilosophy

    An excuse invented to save a claim from contrary evidence.

    AllostasisPsychology

    regulating the body by anticipating changing demands

    Analytic philosophyPhilosophy

    Style prizing explicit argument, distinctions and formal tools.

    AnattaPhilosophy

    Buddhist non-self, the denial of a permanent independent essence.

    AnchoringPsychology

    The first number biases later estimates.

    Availability heuristicPsychology

    Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind.

    Bad faithPhilosophy

    self-deception that hides situated freedom behind a role or excuse

    Base ratePsychology

    How common something is in the population overall.

    Begging the questionPhilosophy

    Circular reasoning: assuming what you set out to prove.

    BehaviourismPsychology

    Watson and Skinner: study observable behaviour and conditioning.

    BlindsightPsychology

    Responding to visual stimuli without reported awareness of seeing them.

    Bottom-up processingPsychology

    Building perception from raw sensory data.

    Brain in a vatPhilosophy

    Thought experiment: all experience fed in by a computer.

    Cartesian circlePhilosophy

    Using clear ideas to prove God, and God to trust clear ideas.

    Categorical imperativePhilosophy

    Kant's unconditional principle of moral obligation

    Change blindnessPsychology

    Failing to notice large changes in a scene.

    Chinese RoomPhilosophy

    Searle: running the right program is not understanding.

    Clever Hans effectPsychology

    Subjects picking up unintended cues from the experimenter.

    Cocktail party effectPsychology

    Your name cutting through a noisy room.

    CogitoPhilosophy

    "I think, therefore I am": the belief doubt cannot touch.

    Cognitive revolutionPsychology

    1950s-70s return to studying memory, language and thought.

    CompatibilismPhilosophy

    The view that causal determination can coexist with a meaningful kind of free will.

    ConfoundPsychology

    A hidden third variable that explains an apparent link.

    Continental philosophyPhilosophy

    Phenomenology, existentialism, critical theory: experience, history, power.

    Correspondence biasPsychology

    The tendency to infer a stable trait from behaviour while underusing situational information.

    CounterexamplePhilosophy

    A single case that breaks a general claim.

    DeductionPhilosophy

    Certain conclusions from premises, if they are true.

    Default mode networkPsychology

    Brain network active during mind-wandering and self-reflection.

    Demarcation problemPhilosophy

    Where to draw the line between science and non-science.

    Double-blindPsychology

    Neither participants nor experimenters know who got what.

    Duhem-Quine thesisPhilosophy

    Hypotheses are always tested together with background assumptions.

    Ecological rationalityPsychology

    Gigerenzer: a heuristic's quality depends on its environment.

    Effect sizePsychology

    How big an effect is, not just whether it exists.

    Engaged followershipPsychology

    Active commitment to an authority or cause judged to be worthy, rather than passive obedience.

    EnthymemePhilosophy

    An argument with an unstated, hidden premise.

    Epistemic luckPhilosophy

    Being right for the wrong reasons.

    Epistemic vigilancePhilosophy

    Cognitive and social checks on the reliability of messages and their sources.

    EpistemologyPhilosophy

    The theory of knowledge and justified belief.

    Eudaimonic well-beingPsychology

    flourishing through purpose, growth, agency and relationships

    Expected utilityPhilosophy

    the probability-weighted value of possible outcomes

    Experienced well-beingPsychology

    feelings measured during or close to the moments they occur

    Explicit vs implicit memoryPsychology

    Facts and events you can state vs skills and habits you show.

    Facial action unitPsychology

    a coded visible muscle movement used in facial-expression research

    FallibilismPhilosophy

    Knowledge without absolute certainty.

    FalsifiabilityPhilosophy

    A claim is scientific if some observation could show it false.

    fMRIPsychology

    Imaging blood oxygen changes as a slow proxy for brain activity.

    Forgetting curvePsychology

    Ebbinghaus: rapid early forgetting that then levels off.

    FoundationalismPhilosophy

    Knowledge rests on certain, basic foundations.

    Framing effectPsychology

    Equivalent options chosen differently depending on wording.

    FunctionalismPsychology

    William James: what the mind is for.

    GestaltPsychology

    Organising perception into wholes: figure-ground, proximity, closure.

    Gettier casePhilosophy

    A justified true belief that is true only by luck.

    Global workspace theoryPsychology

    Consciousness as information broadcast across the brain.

    Group polarisationPsychology

    A shift after discussion toward a more extreme version of the group's initial average.

    Hard problemPhilosophy

    Why physical processing comes with experience at all.

    HARKingPsychology

    Hypothesising after the results are known.

    HeuristicPsychology

    A fast mental shortcut that is usually good enough.

    HEXACOPsychology

    A six-factor personality model including honesty-humility.

    Identity leadershipPsychology

    Leading by defining a shared group identity and what that identity requires.

    Inattentional blindnessPsychology

    Missing an obvious object when attention is elsewhere.

    InductionPhilosophy

    Probable generalisations from observed cases.

    Interaction problemPhilosophy

    How a non-physical mind could move a physical body.

    InteroceptionPsychology

    sensing the body's internal state, such as heartbeat or breath

    JunziPhilosophy

    the exemplary person formed through learning, ritual and relationships

    Justified true beliefPhilosophy

    The classic three-part definition of knowledge.

    Levels of explanationPsychology

    Cell, circuit, person, group and culture accounts of one behaviour.

    Limbic systemPsychology

    Amygdala, hippocampus and hypothalamus: emotion and memory.

    LogicPhilosophy

    The study of which inferences preserve truth or support.

    MetaethicsPhilosophy

    the study of what moral claims mean and whether moral facts exist

    MetaphysicsPhilosophy

    What is real: mind, self, time, causation, God.

    Method of doubtPhilosophy

    Descartes: reject any belief that could possibly be false.

    Misinformation effectPsychology

    Post-event suggestions blending into a memory.

    Moral foundationsPsychology

    psychological dimensions proposed to organise recurring moral concerns

    MysterianismPhilosophy

    The view that humans may never solve the mind-body problem.

    NeuroplasticityPsychology

    The brain's lifelong capacity to rewire with experience.

    Nishkama karmaPhilosophy

    acting from duty without attachment to the fruits of action

    Occam's razorPhilosophy

    Prefer fewer assumptions, explanatory power held fixed.

    Operational definitionPsychology

    The exact procedure used to measure a concept.

    p-hackingPsychology

    Trying analyses until a result crosses p < .05.

    ParadigmPhilosophy

    Kuhn: the shared framework a scientific field works within.

    Perceptual setPsychology

    A mental readiness to perceive one thing over another.

    PhilPapers SurveyPhilosophy

    2009 and 2020 surveys of what professional philosophers believe.

    PhronesisPhilosophy

    practical wisdom that judges what a situation calls for

    PhysicalismPhilosophy

    Everything, minds included, is physical or depends on the physical.

    PramanaPhilosophy

    Indian philosophy: a reliable source of knowledge (perception, inference, testimony...).

    Predictive processingPsychology

    The brain as a prediction machine corrected by sensory error signals.

    PremisePhilosophy

    A reason offered in support of a conclusion.

    PreregistrationPsychology

    Recording hypotheses and analyses before seeing data.

    Problem of inductionPhilosophy

    Hume: no non-circular justification for expecting the future to resemble the past.

    Psychological continuityPhilosophy

    Overlapping mental connections, such as memory, intention and character, linked through time.

    PurusarthasPhilosophy

    dharma, artha, kama and moksha as a plural map of human pursuits

    QualiaPhilosophy

    What an experience feels like from the inside.

    Random assignmentPsychology

    Assigning conditions by chance so groups are comparable.

    Readiness potentialPsychology

    An EEG potential that tends to precede self-initiated movement in averaged data.

    ReconsolidationPsychology

    A retrieved memory becoming editable before re-storage.

    Regression to the meanPsychology

    Extreme results tend to be followed by more average ones.

    ReliabilismPhilosophy

    Knowledge as belief produced by a reliable process.

    RenPhilosophy

    Confucian humaneness or humane, authoritative conduct

    Replication crisisPsychology

    2011-15 discovery that many famous findings did not reproduce.

    RepresentativenessPsychology

    Judging by resemblance to a type, neglecting base rates.

    ScepticismPhilosophy

    Doubt about whether we can know some or all things.

    Seductive allurePsychology

    Bad explanations seem better with irrelevant neuroscience added.

    Selective attentionPsychology

    Focusing on one input and filtering the rest.

    Socratic methodPhilosophy

    Cross-examining someone to expose hidden assumptions.

    SoundPhilosophy

    Valid with all premises actually true.

    SteelmanPhilosophy

    The strongest version of the opposing view.

    StructuralismPsychology

    Wundt and Titchener: breaking experience into elements.

    Substance dualismPhilosophy

    Mind and body as two different kinds of thing.

    System 1 / System 2Psychology

    Kahneman's metaphor for fast intuition and slow deliberation.

    Top-down processingPsychology

    Expectations and knowledge shaping perception.

    UnfalsifiabilityPhilosophy

    A structure that prevents any possible observation from counting against a claim.

    ValidPhilosophy

    If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be.

    Value theoryPhilosophy

    Ethics, political philosophy and aesthetics.

    Variable-ratio schedulePsychology

    Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses.

    WEIRDPsychology

    Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic samples.

    Colophon

    Notice it. Question it. Use it.
